title: The bark that returns: cork harvest as a material cycle
deck: Cork oak can rebuild its protective bark after careful harvest, creating an unusual renewable material system whose benefits still depend on skilled management and viable woodlands.

sections.heading: Harvesting without felling
sections.text: Cork is the outer bark of the cork oak, Quercus suber. Skilled stripping removes harvestable bark while leaving the living tissues that allow a new protective layer to form, distinguishing cork from timber extraction.

sections.heading: The tree and its range
sections.text: Kew recognises Quercus suber as an accepted species native to parts of the western Mediterranean. Botanical distribution describes species occurrence and should not be confused with the geography of processing industries.

sections.heading: A slow working calendar
sections.text: Kew notes that bark is harvested manually at intervals measured in years rather than seasons. The cycle depends on tree maturity, bark growth and regulation, and a careless cut can damage tissues needed for recovery.

sections.heading: Light, cellular and compressible
sections.text: Cork’s cellular structure helps explain its low density, resilience and insulating behaviour. Those properties support closures as well as flooring, panels and products that require cushioning or thermal separation.

sections.heading: Material and managed woodland
sections.text: FAO documentation places cork production within managed forest landscapes. Continued ecological value is not automatic: it depends on regeneration, fire risk, grazing, labour, markets and management choices.

sections.heading: Renewable is not impact-free
sections.text: The bark’s capacity to regrow supports a renewable cycle, but it does not make every cork product or supply chain sustainable by definition. Transport, processing, adhesives, harvest practice and land management still require evidence.
